speechtext:
It is not going to be that good. The position of this party has been that we are not trying to invade the constitutional responsibilities of the province. I noticed that the Leader of the Opposition, while in Winnipeg over the weekend, accused the government of seeking confrontation with the province of Quebec and therefore worsening the separatist situation. I noticed that the young New Democrats also accused the federal government of holding the province of Quebec in a colonial status and stated that we should not continue this overbearing position.
I submit that the amendment proposed by the opposition along the lines of establishing such a commission would precisely be doing that, seeking confrontation with the province of Quebec in a matter of its jurisdiction and, as the New Democratic Party suggests, treating the province of Quebec as a colony. The position of this government has consistently been that in matters of provincial jurisdiction such as the administration of justice, the province would not be looked upon by the federal government as a Big Brother to see whether it does its job well. The resolution adopted by the convention stated in the final part that a way must be sought to do this without infringing upon provincial autonomy. We have found no way of doing what is suggested without appearing or in fact endeavouring to oversee the province of Quebec in its rightful operations.
I must add that the Minister of Justice and I have both had communications with the authorities of Quebec. Twice today I spoke with Premier Bourassa trying to find a way in which we would at least be able to go some distance in ensuring that a statutory committee would be established to consider the application of this Act in Quebec. Mr. Chairman, in light of what the Prime Minister said today in response to questions from the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Calgary North and others, I think we have to review this situation because in my view the Prime Minister has misinformed the House as to what the issue really is. There is no question at all about the distribution of powers between the provinces and the federal government with regard to civil law. That is set out very clearly. Section 91(27) of the B.N.A. Act provides that the federal government shall have jurisdiction in respect of:
The criminal law, except the constitution of courts of Criminal Jurisdiction, but including the procedure in criminal matters.
The Depuiy Chairman: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but I would like to remind hon. members that they should hold their private conversations outside the chamber so that other interested members might listen to the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River.

I quite agree with you, Mr. Chairman. I assumed that a great many members thought they were still in the more jovial circumstances of yesterday and the day before.
There is that clear and precise definition of the jurisdiction of the federal government. For a great many years, the Criminal Code of this country has made it absolutely clear that questions with regard to bail lie exclusively under the jurisdiction of the federal government. There are a number of sections, from section 463 on of the Criminal Code, which constitute a code dealing with this issue of bail. On this issue of bail, as is proper, jurisdiction has been given by the federal government to the courts and to a judge. What the Prime Minister said today, and what the Minister of Justice said previously, in my view indicates that there is a cowardly skulking behind a misinterpretation of the constitution. That is the situation, nothing more and nothing less.
Certainly, in so far as this bill we are now dealing with creates new criminal offences, the Prime Minister is absolutely right. The procedure in connection with the administration of justice lies within the hands of the provincial government, and under the special aegis of the
Public Order Act, 1970
provincial attorney general. So it does, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the question of arresting without warrant. But every one of the problems posed by this new legislation, every one of the remedies sought by this party for the purpose of trying to provide some form of safeguard, ultimately comes back to the question of bail.
When the federal Parliament presumes by this bill to take away from the courts and put in the hands of a provincial attorney general the right to say whether or not bail shall be granted, which is the total effect of the provisions I am referring to, it is not proper. In fact, it is wrong for the Prime Minister and for the Minister of Justice to say that this is a matter which lies squarely within the jurisdiction of the provincial attorney general. He is given that extraordinary power because it has been taken away from the courts. This amendment proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North asks, if you take this extraordinary step of depriving courts and judges of the right of deciding whether or not bail shall be granted and give that power to the attorney general of the province, then why not have a means for reviewing that procedure? That is all we are asking.

I suggest that the statements made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice bear no resemblance to the facts and no resemblance to the law. The Liberal convention was a little wiser than they in urging this sort of review process in respect of bail. That is the essence of one of the great contributions to criminal law in this country and the United Kingdom, the right of a person charged with an offence and detained in custody to go to court and seek bail. He is brought before a J.P. or a supreme or county court judge; the question of bail is argued and the attorney general, through his agent, is a party to the proceedings. The attorney general can argue against bail because of the nature of the offence or, if bail is to be fixed, he can ask that it be in an amount large enough to ensure the appearance of the accused at the time of trial.
This government wants to take this right away from the courts and put it in the hands of the attorney general. To say that this is the constitutional right of the attorney general under the British North America Act is absolute drivel, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Justice knows that and so does the Prime Minister, or they should know it.
All we are asking is that the kind of safeguard in respect of the granting of bail which, since time immemorial, has been intertwined with the principles of criminal law in this country, be maintained. I can only assume, by reason of their obstinacy and obduracy, that this government long ago entered into a secret covenant with the province of Quebec not to change this bill one iota. This is the only inference I can draw from this refusal to agree to this very reasonable proposal.

Of course, we had been assured that within the next few days, special legislation would be submitted, with the participation of Parliament. We were told that after taking into consideration suggestions emanating from all political parties, a special legislation, adapted to today's needs, albeit of a temporary nature, would be brought forward.
It seems to me that the participation of Parliament was not very significant. The bill was introduced and, if I am not mistaken, not a single amendment has been accepted by the government.
Of course, this bill affects Quebec in a particular way, since the problem under discussion exists in the province of Quebec.
I did not want to miss the opportunity to discuss the proposed amendment. It has been said earlier that the opposition has been trying for several days to demolish the bill clause by clause. On the contrary, the proposed amendment does not change anything at all in the wording of the clause put forward by the government. Why do they refuse to establish a commission or a supervisory committee, or to appoint an administrator-which would amount to the same thing and change nothing at all in the bill-in order to give the innocent people who have been annoyed without reason by the War Measures Act the assurance that the special measure now before the House will not have the same effect for them?
As a Quebec member who has studied seriously the wording of the act, I wonder if the federal government can intrude in the affairs of the provinces. At any rate, it seems that the general wording of the act which will be applied everywhere in Canada does not include any dis-

tinction on this matter. The act must be enforced everywhere in Canada. It is not even wondered if Quebec will accept it or not. The duty of the administrator would be to prevent abuses. I have the clear impression that this is only an assurance.
In my opinion, this is not a lack of confidence in the Quebec Minister of Justice or in the persons responsible for the administration of justice, because of the temporary nature of the act. The application of the War Measures Act has nevertheless permitted the arrest of many persons, in Quebec, for serious reasons and, sometimes, for not so serious reasons. power to appoint other people to be administrators in order to investigate and remedy abuses which may arise as a result of the implementation of this measure. The amendment also gives the administrators the power to review and confirm, vary or revoke a certificate filed by an attorney general where someone may be put in jail for 90 days. If the attorney general files a certificate that the man is there for just cause or reason, then that is it. Of course, it is very easy to do this because it just involves a matter of bureaucracy.
What we are asking is very simple. We are asking for review machinery very similar to that suggested in the amendment moved by the NDP, except we may have gone a little further by suggesting that the administrators would be members of the judiciary. I agree with what has been said in this regard. We do not care about the makeup of this review board. All we want to have is a review board to be used against abuse.
The question to ask today is what evidence is there of abuse. Just before answering that question, let me say that I cannot believe we can have this kind of legislation administered by any human being in office anywhere in Canada, whether it be within provincial or federal jurisdiction, without there being some abuse. We must come back to the premise that the only protection the individual has is that given under the rule of law. Without that protection, we have no protection.
Has there been abuse to date? We know there have been abuses. We know this by the number of arrests and the number of people who have been detained without charge under the War Measures Act or under the Criminal Code. We know that Gerard Lortie, a student in Hull, was picked up, even though he had voluntarily given his name to the police. He told them he was not the man they were looking for but thought he better tell them he had the same name. We know from reading the newspapers he was held in custody, and that is the only way we can get facts from this government. We know he was held incommunicado for a period of time without the right to retain counsel or see his parents, even though they went to Montreal. We know the door of the house occupied by the Secretary of State was kicked in. If he had not been the Secretary of State he might have been thrown in jail.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to emphasize the obvious failure of the government to be responsive and responsible, even in the face of the

expressed wishes of its own party supporters. That fact has been well documented. The amount of obstinacy that can be seen in a government is really incredible, when it will not even listen to the group of people one would most expect to support the position it had taken. The fact that the rank and file of the government party's supporters at a national meeting could indicate, by majority vote, that the government had failed in a very grave way to respond to the request for a review clause in this bill is nothing short of shocking.
What is just as shocking is the misleading impression created by the government, both in this House and throughout the country, that it was prepared to deal with this issue on the broadest possible front in the belief that a united stand in this House, or as close to it as could be approximated, would be important in resolving the question. Therefore, in dealing with the regulations under the War Measures Act, both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice made it very clear there would be a process of consultation with regard to the drafting of legislation to be submitted as a temporary public order bill. As is well known, some consultation did occur. However, I believe even the Minister of Justice will confirm the fact that during the periods of consultation prior to the introduction of this bill he was not able to provide a detailed summation of what the bill would contain.
Now that the bill has been introduced, we have seen a complete unwillingness on the part of the government to continue what was supposed to have been a policy of constructive consultation. There has been an unwillingness on the part of the government to accept the amendments presented by the NDP and by my party at their face value, as being important and reasonable contributions to the bill. Not only has there been an unwillingness to do so, but there has been a stubbornness that has been nothing short of unbelievable with respect to this important piece of legislation. Surely the process of consultation which took place before the introduction of the bill must now be considered a farce by most people because the government has proven itself unwilling to consult on the most important details of the bill. To say the least, it has shown a willingness to hide behind arguments that are unsound, arguments that do not in any way face the facts.
As recently as this afternoon, the Prime Minister has argued that to place a review clause in the legislation would call the competency of the provincial government into question. I would think that is a total misreading of the responsibilities of this House and of the joint jurisdiction that exists with regard to the courts and the processes of justice. As has been emphasized by the hon. member for Calgary North, through this amendment we are not asking for a review body that could only be viewed as some kind of federal intervention. What we are seeking is an assurance, under law, that there will be a review board which will ensure that justice is not only being done but will be seen to be done. The fact that the government refuses to respond in any reasonable fashion to that request must make this legislation not only dubious but in direct opposition to the best interests of the people of the country.

November 23, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
Time and time again within the past few days the Minister of Justice has argued that we must be prepared to allow particular anomalies in this legislation such as retroactivity, the provision that might allow a husband or wife to give evidence against a spouse, and the provision with respect to the period of time that a person may be kept in jail before he is brought before a court. Time and time again he has said that because of the nature of the situation, because of the grave difficulties in Quebec, because of the crisis, these are temporary and special powers that the government would not normally seek, but which it must ask for in this instance.
I am not saying that I have accepted that argument, but at least it is the one that the Minister of Justice has put forward. It is one with which he feels comfortable. If that is an argument on behalf of special powers which, to use the words of the right hon. member for Prince Albert, place the rights of many Canadians in cold storage for a period of time, why is the minister not willing to ask for special assurances, for a special review board, and for a special protection under the law so that the abuses to which reference has been made could not in fact take place? It seems unreasonable to me that on the one hand the minister would ask for these special and extraordinary powers, and on the other hand not be willing to examine with his cabinet colleagues, and with the authorities in Quebec, special and extraordinary powers to protect abuses under this legislation. In short, he is asking for a very special and extraordinary privilege without introducing the kind of guarantees and protection which we in this House have a right to expect.
Our debate on this bill, even that part of it dealing with the question of a review board, may seem somewhat remote to people generally throughout the country. However, I think it is important to let them know that we are acting in their best interests, that we are in fact ensuring that justice will be done. Editorial after editorial has supported our position. The party which supports the government, the people who have given overwhelming support to the government for introducing the War Measures Act regulations and this temporary public order bill, have said that at the very least there must be some kind of review commission to ensure that not only will justice be done but that it will be seen to be done.
In arguing this afternoon along the kind of arid, and in this instance somewhat theoretic line about constitutional interference, the Prime Minister has avoided facing the basic questions involved in this issue. He has misled the House and misled the people into believing that the matter of constitutional haggling is more important than justice being done for millions and millions of people in this country.
Anyone who has examined what has happened under the administration of the War Measures Act regulations, anyone who is aware that more than 80 per cent of the people arrested were subsequently released without being charged, must realize that more people are going to be arrested, detained and searched who really in no way, shape or form are related to the acts of terrorism involved. My third question is this: Is this really a right wing law and order bill designed to appease the sabre rattlers throughout Canada, the ones who see in all change a symbol of creeping permissiveness to be stamped out forthwith. I wish to propose an amendment to clause 15 of the bill. I propose to extend to Parliament the right that the government now holds of limiting the period of the enforcement of the bill to April 30, 1971. At present clause 15 reads:
This Act expires on the 30th day of April, 1971 or on such earlier day as may he fixed by proclamation, unless before the 30th day of April, 1971 or before any earlier day fixed by proclamation, both Houses of Parliament, by joint resolution, direct that this Act shall continue in force until a day specified in the resolution, in which case this Act expires on that specified day.
My amendment is as follows. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North:
That section 15 be amended by adding the following words as subjection (2),
(2) a Notice of Motion in either house signed by ten members thereof and made in accordance with the rules of that house, praying that an earlier day for the expiry of this Act shall be fixed by proclamation, shall be debated in that house at the first convenient opportunity within four sitting days after notice thereof is given, and renumbering the first paragraph of Section 15"(1)".
I have two copies of this particular amendment for distribution. In 1969, Mr. Chairman, the Bill of Rights contained an amendment affecting the War Measures Act and asserted the right of Parliament, for the first time, to fix an earlier date for the suspension of that act if any ten members should signify their intention in writing to hold a debate. We know that clause 15 contains a paradox, in that Parliament has the right to extend the special powers beyond April 30, but only the government can shorten the period. This, as I have said, is wrong, because Parliament ought not to be placed in a position that is subordinate to the duly elected autocracy.
There are two conditions under which I think Parliament can invoke the right to "pray for an earlier expiry". I think I have used the correct words. One of those
conditions involves police excesses and injustices, of which we have heard a great deal this afternoon and on previous days. There must be, as I said, police excesses and injustices causing mental and physical anguish to those arrested on suspicion only. When those conditions exist, Parliament ought to invoke the right requested. The second condition involves the lack of demonstrable need, because of a return to normalcy in Quebec, that the civil rights of all Canadians which are unnecessarily being restricted should be withheld no longer. Under those conditions Parliament ought to avail itself of this right to end the special powers as unnecessary.
I hope that the minister and his colleagues will consider this amendment. Last week the minister said that the invocation of the special powers and the consequent loss of personal freedom was based on a value judgment. He indicated that the government was prepared to take the risk consequent upon this value judgment. That is all very well. I know this, and every Canadian knows and is prepared to accept this. There is to be some loss of freedom. The value judgment tells us that much. It is not the loss of freedom we object to; we want to know how great will be the loss of freedom, and for how long a time. In order to meet the need, and in order to meet this real or imaginary challenge to the state, we must be prepared, as we have said we are, to lose some freedom. That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of providing loans and grants to encourage the building and improvement of fishing facilities along the Atlantic coastlines for the better collection and storage of all marketable species of fish.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am putting forward this motion today because I have witnessed the unnecessary loss of livelihood by fishermen in my own district, and I presume a similar situation confronts fishermen in other parts of the Atlantic provinces. I was prompted to submit this motion because of a situation which exists in my district which takes in some 250 miles of coastline and embraces many small fishing communities which depend solely on the inshore cod fishery. During the season when the fishermen are fishing for cod many other species of fish, including flounder, mackerel, herring and salmon, are attracted to the nets. Since the fish plant on which the fishermen must depend to buy their fish is only prepared to accept the cod, the fishermen have to throw back the other species of fish and loss of income results. Along 200 miles of the northwest coast, which I represent, there is only one fish plant and during the season it is only able to handle the cod.

In one community last year when codfish were very scarce, the fishermen of the community as well as others had literally to discard thousands of pounds of other species of fish because the fish plant could not handle them. Strangely enough, many of the other species of fish are worth much more than cod, and the fishermen were deterred from selling this fish due to lack of storage and cooling or freezing facilities where the fish could be kept for other markets.
Many buyers in the provinces are prepared to buy other species of fish but cannot be on hand immediately it is caught. Nevertheless they are ready to handle it if the facilities are satisfactory. The federal government, in co-operation with the provincial government, are now granting up to 90 per cent of the cost of a long liner under their boat building program, and it is very evident that codfish stocks are being depleted. This would enable them to market the other species of fish by building small holding units with cooling and freezing facilities to keep the product at the proper temperature for sale to the market.
I have visited the industrial development branch of the Department of Fisheries and Forestry and have seen

I have also found in my visits to fishing communities that much government money is being wasted by building wharves and breakwaters on contract. A great saving could be effected if this type of fishing facility were built by the fishermen themselves under the supervision of the engineering staff of the Department of Public Works.
The fisherman in Newfoundland has the native ability and knowledge, passed on through generations, to know where and how a breakwater should be built for the greater benefit of all concerned. I have seen too many hundreds of thousands of dollars wasted on breakwaters and wharves which were built for political advantage, of no avail to the fishermen concerned and at too great a cost to the taxpayer.
If I can quote another example of taking other species of fish, through the initiative of the industrial development branch of the Department of Fisheries great value has been placed on lump spawn, and a market for this spawn has been found in Germany and other countries. Through this branch of the department a buyer from Germany came to Newfoundland and contracted to purchase lump spawn, which previously was not even considered of any value. For this spawn the fishermen is paid more than twice what he gets for cod; but again lack of cooling facilities prevents him from taking advantage of the market for this type of product, with the result that again he loses a source of income. I know of other experiences where fish buyers refused to buy salmon from the fisherman in his community due to lack of ice. Upwards of a hundred men could have been employeer if the facilities to store the salmon and prepare it for market had been available.
Irish moss is another product which the government spent many dollars to find; yet the market for a new product which brings income to fishermen has gradually deteriorated due to the fact that proper facilities are not available. The government for some reason or other will not realize that studies and surveys must be supported by facilities to take advantage of a product.
How many times do I get replies from the Department of Public Works to my requests for breakwaters and wharves and dredging to the effect that, since the catch and the number of fishermen are decreasing in a particular community, there can be no justification to spend the money? Little do they realize-or they do not want to realize-that the reason for the decrease in the catch and the number of fishermen is that there are no facilities in the first place.
It is time we gave our fishermen some credit for initiative and decision to an industry which is the lifeline of my province. In this fast advancing age of science and technology all they require is a little guidance and assistance. I am sure that my motion would have the support

May I suggest respectfully that there be a few test cases at strategic locations in the Atlantic provinces which depend on the fishery to evaluate the proposal which I put forward today, and I hope that I will have the support of my other colleagues who must have experienced like circumstances in their districts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I compliment the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for his interest in, and concern for, the fisheries which are so vital to Newfoundland and to the welfare of Newfoundland fishermen. The Department of Fisheries and Forestry is, and always has been, acutely concerned with the improvement of facilities to enable fishermen to handle their catch and to expand and diversify their operations. The department has programs along this line and others designed, in one way or another, to increase fishermen's incomes and to improve their standard of living.
Many changes are presently underway that directly or indirectly affect the orderly development of the fisheries in Newfoundland. Resettlement, improved transportation, the swing from the salted to the frozen product, the harvesting of new or under-exploited species and stocks, and new catching and processing techniques, are just a few examples.
These factors make it difficult to come to hard and firm decisions about the location and type of facilities for handling fish. In the past we have built community stages at suitable places where fishermen can handle their own fish, especially for salting. There is now the feeling that fishermen should devote their full time to fishing-which is, of course, their principal occupation and the thing that they do best-and have their catches processed by workers at appropriate shore facilities. This would tend to produce more uniform and better quality salt fish.
Recently the government announced an expansion of its fishing vessel construction assistance. Under the new regulations, financial assistance-35 per cent of the approved cost-will be provided for eligible fishing vessels of all types built of any materials, 45 feet in length and over. For vessels 45 feet to 75 feet in length, funds in the amount of $2 million have been appropriated by the Department of Fisheries and Forestry, and applications from vessel owners are now under consideration.
For vessels more than 75 feet in length, assistance is available through the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce by way of grants paid directly to shipyards after approval by the Department of Fisheries and Forestry. An expenditure of $3 million is projected for this
program. This assistance is helpful in enabling fishermen to obtain larger, more up to date and more mobile boats which will make it possible for them to use different kinds of gear and catch additional species of fish, and, through this diversification, allow them to extend their fishing season. All these factors, details of which I will provide in a moment, may mean that we shall eventually have fewer but better serviced fishing centres for better boats where there will be improved unloading and handling facilities, better wharfing, haul-out and so on.
e (5:10 p.m.)
In the program for community fish processing and handling facilities, federal expenditure between the fiscal year 1953-54 and 1968-69 amounted to $4 million. Fifty-three community stages for saltfish were built, and 22 fresh fish holding units, as well as related marine works. The purpose was to meet the problems of Newfoundland fishermen in previous years, such as low individual productivity and indifferent quality of fish produced. In addition to the Newfoundland program, two fresh fish holding units were constructed in Nova Scotia and one in New Brunswick.
The department reviews the operation of this program every year with a view to assessing the use made of the individual units and the benefits accruing to fishermen. With some exceptions, the program is felt to have met its purpose in Newfoundland. As I intimated, no new community stage program is planned for the current year.
There are instances where some kind of facilities such as those proposed by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe-something perhaps more elaborate than a community stage for fresh fish holding unit- would be desirable.
The 1970 report of Imbucon Services, a firm of consultants, recommends consideration of a program of licensed landing centres for the inshore fishery, a place for receiving fish and providing a number of services to fishermen. Part of the costs of the proposed operation might be covered in part by a levy on all fish moved over a dock serviced by the unit.
In co-operation with various provincial administrations the department undertakes fisheries development programs on a joint share basis. From April 1, 1962 to March 31, 1971 federal contributions in the Atlantic coast provinces will total just over $6 million, of which $2,758,000 will have been spent in Newfoundland. I should like to include details of these expenditures along with my remarks. Perhaps I might have the indulgence of the House to table these figures, Mr. Speaker.

We had hoped that he would have addressed himself to the motion because it is a very important one, underlining as it does a serious deficiency in the Department of Fisheries and Forestry for which the Parliamentary Secretary now has some responsibility.
Every year in my constituency we have the spectacle of hundreds of thousands of pounds of fish being dumped into the water because there is no space to hold them until buyers can be found and the fish can be transported to market. This resolution merely calls upon the government to provide these facilities and, in effect, preclude the necessity for this terrible waste of a very valuable high protein food. There are many fishermen within the city of St. John's, and a number of fishermen in the small areas surrounding St. John's, but there are no fish plants: there are only two small units to receive the catches. There were two large plants in the city itself but they were forced to close because of market conditions and other factors of which I am not fully aware.
Certainly, if cold storage units were built at strategic points along the coasts of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-and X offer my own constituency as an example-it would preclude this terrible waste of high protein food and would help the fishermen. The catch could be held until it was determined whether there was a market for it. Fish is a very perishable product, and under the present circumstances, if no buyer is immediately available there is no alternative but to dump it and the fishermen is in the unhappy position of labouring for naught.
This is a very serious matter, Mr. Speaker, and I regret that the Parliamentary Secretary did not seem to comprehend its importance. I do not think things have changed very much, Mr. Speaker. Actually, in these areas we are moving a little faster than before. The motion before the House deals with an important aspect of the fishery, namely, collection and cold storage facilities. Although important, it deals with only one aspect of a very complex activity. This activity is broader than that with which the motion on the Order Paper attempts to deal. These cold storage facilities are closely related to the number and location of fishermen, the number and size of fishing vessels used by fishermen, the volume of the catch, the availability of harbour facilities, the location of processing plants, and so on.
Moreover, the Atlantic coast fishery is experiencing significant changes. Fishing effort is increasingly oriented toward deep sea activity, with larger and more sophisticated fishing vessels, while inshore fishing is receding in importance. As the previous speaker said, there is still a great deal of inshore fishing and we should like to see a change in this area. As he pointed out, we can provide subsidies for sophisticated fishing vessels and encourage their construction. In addition, Mr. Speaker, more of the catch is being processed into fresh and frozen fillets and less is being cured. Also, more landings are concentrated in locations with large processing plants.

It must be readily apparent that it would not be wise to adopt a new general policy to provide for better collection and cold storage facilities, let alone a set level and amount of financial assistance, until we can see where it fits into the general fisheries development policy. The definition of such a policy will incorporate the matter of collection and storage facilities. The prime responsibility of fisheries development, of course, lies with the Department of Fisheries and Forestry. However, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has since its inception had a direct interest in this significant regional economic activity.
Several of DREE's activities are specifically oriented toward the Atlantic coast fishery. Financial assistance is available for new fish processing plants and for the modernization and expansion of existing plants under the Regional Development Incentives Act. Assistance provided under this program since July 1, 1969, amounts to $1.7 million. The federal-provincial agreements under the fund for regional economic development for northeast New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island also included substantial fisheries development programs. DREE is also contributing in a significant manner to the development and rationalization of the Newfoundland fishery by way of the Newfoundland resettlement program. Again, DREE is at present negotiating renewals of ARDA agreements with the provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

I admit that the adamant and contemptuous attitude which my amendments met with made me lose my temper at times, and on some occasions my words went beyond my thoughts. CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-NON-PAYMENT OF MINIMUM WAGE-RETIRED EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS- GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 4 I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mack-asey) a question regarding the payment of less than the minimum federal wage to employees of the Chateau Laurier Hotel in Ottawa. The minister replied:
I expressed this opinion two weeks ago and gave my department the authority to proceed in the matter in the usual manner. I refer to the application of the rules and regulations under which the Department of Labour normally proceeds in
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
such cases. I presume that advice is now being sought from the appropriate department in regard to proceeding further.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question dealt with the Canadian National pension plan. But speaking first to the original question put to the Minister of Labour, it appears at this time, which is more than two weeks after November 4, that the situation at the Chateau Laurier Hotel has not been clarified. It is my information that there is hesitation on the part of some departments of government to take any action to find out whether the Chateau Laurier Hotel falls within federal or provincial jurisdiction. It is very ironic, to say the least, that at one time the CNR Chateau Laurier Hotel was quite prepared to be within federal jurisdiction so far as the payment of wages and other conditions were concerned, but now that the federal minimum wage is more than the provincial minimum wage they have the audacity to suggest that they are under provincial jurisdiction.
Even though there may be a case in Canada-I understand there is one in Alberta in respect of Jasper Lodge- regarding whether or not a certificate of collective bargaining can be granted under provincial or federal legislation, I cannot understand why the appropriate department of government will not move in respect of the Chateau Laurier Hotel and decide that it should be governed by federal legislation.
A supplementary question was asked of the minister in respect of the CNR pension plan. In view of the CNR labour-management question which is before the country, and the fact that labour is asking that pensions be put on the bargaining table, I think it is only right that we be assured that the CNR will consider putting its pension plan on the bargaining table.
We are aware that the unanimous report of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, which in effect took no position concerning collective bargaining, suggested that persons already on pension should be given the same consideration that pensioners received some time ago. At the same time it was suggested that there should be an escalator clause. This suggestion received the unanimous agreement of the House of Commons. It would seem appropriate therefore, that a minister should answer to the House in respect of whether Canadian National plans to do something similar about its pension plan. I am given to understand that Canadian National has communicated with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), but neither the Minister of Labour nor the Parliamentary Secretary would be in a position to answer for the Minister of Transport so I shall defer that question until another time. The most important questions at this time are why the Chateau Laurier is not paying the federal minimum wage, and why no action is being taken on the part of the Canadian National management to act at least in part on the recommendations of the committee which were adopted unanimously so far as pension plan is concerned.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Perrauli (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-NON-PAYMENT OF MINIMUM WAGE-RETIRED EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS- GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, within its jurisdiction, this

November 23, 1970
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
government is determined to provide decent wage standards lor the working people of Canada. While 30 per cent of Canadian workers are organized, the percentage stands at 50 per cent in those industries within federal jurisdiction. Many workers, particularly in the unorganized sector, are in low-paying jobs. Some time ago the federal government established minimum wage legislation. Periodically, this federal minimum wage has been increased. Today it stands at $1.65 an hour, the highest in Canada.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) believes it is a major responsibility of the government to continue to assure, by law, an adequate minimum wage and to secure compliance with the rules and regulations which form the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. The Department of Labour and the minister support the view that Crown corporations like the CNR are bound to comply with the federal minimum wage legislation, as are all other industries coming within federal jurisdiction.
A short while ago the minister instructed his officials to proceed with action designed to establish beyond all doubt the obligation of the CNR to pay at least the federal minimum wage. It is not the minister's prerogative to determine in law whether federal minimum wage statutes apply to all phases of Canadian National operations. Without any doubt, however, if legal ambiguities are resolved in favour of federal jurisdiction, the Minister of Labour will continue to enforce vigorously federal minimum wage provisions on behalf of all Canadian National employees.
With respect to the hon. member's other observations, the Department of Labour shares with him a hope that the outstanding differences between the CNR and its employees will be resolved satisfactorily. The minister has stated in this House that the report of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications should be required reading, not only by the CNR but also by the unions in view of the report's wide-ranging recommendations for both management and labour.
One current dispute between the CNR and the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers is at the conciliation stage, as is a dispute between the CPR and the same union. Other disputes between the CNR and the unions representing most other categories of railway employees are at the direct negotiation stage, that is, no conciliation officer or board has been appointed. The specific question of pensions is dealt with in the demands presented by most unions involved in the current negotiations. The Department of Labour's industry specialist, Mr. Arthur Gibbons, is keeping in very close touch with the parties and the proceedings. The government is sure that both parties realize the importance of the negotiations. I thank the hon. member for directing these important inquiries to the Department of Labour.

INQUIRY OF THE MINISTRY-GENERAL DE GAULLE'S FUNERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I asked last week was rather important although it was received with indifference by the Right Hon. Prime
Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Since 1968 we have been getting used to that eloquent silence which is a manifestation of the childish and offhand streak in his personality. The carnations (oeillets) that he often wears in his buttonhole do not make us forget the blinkers (oeilleres) on both sides of his head. He refuses to see anything but his own opinions.

maintopic: INQUIRY OF THE MINISTRY-GENERAL DE GAULLE'S FUNERAL
speechtext:
Why, Mr. Speaker, does the Prime Minister keep silent instead of answering the questions that are put to him? It is a rather simple question. Had he any reasons for refusing to attend General de Gaulle's official funeral? Is it because all the eminent chiefs of State went to Paris on that occasion that the Canadian Prime Minister has not deigned to do so? Does he have any complexes in front of Nixon, Heath, Kosygin, Saragat and the pleiad of other chiefs of State? Does he question the value of the greatest man of contemporary history? Why turn up his nose at the remains of the one who had the last word with such famous men as Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin? Why does he not recognize France's great saviour?
Some concepts of the General undoubtedly gave rise to discussions, if not dissensions, but are those sufficient reasons to show the whole world such pettiness? The President of the United States has not always been in agreement with the General, nor has the British Prime Minister. Yet, they were there. So was the head of the U.S.S.R. Such occasions are surely not the right time for a show of petty spite.
It took a prime minister like ours to dare bring shame to our country. God knows that the prime minister is fond of travelling. He goes here and there, skiing, scub-ba-diving, cruising, etc. He keeps saying that he wants his privacy to be respected. We know how he has run down newspapermen-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: INQUIRY OF THE MINISTRY-GENERAL DE GAULLE'S FUNERAL
speechtext:
Order. I must interrupt the hon. member. I have recognized him for a question and not a speech on the subject of the Prime Minister. The matter before us now is General de Gaulle's funeral and not whether the Prime Minister has answered the question or not.
The hon. member might perhaps on another occasion ask the Prime Minister why he did not answer his question. If there is no answer he will be able to give notice to the Chair and discuss the matter later. At present the matter under consideration is the funeral of General de Gaulle and this has nothing to do with the silence of the Prime Minister.

maintopic: INQUIRY OF THE MINISTRY-GENERAL DE GAULLE'S FUNERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to justify the question.

November 23, 1970

Does the immobility of the Prime Minister on that occasion become as sensational as his social activities and his trips? Never has a country been represented in such a strange way. Therefore it is important that we should be told the true reasons of his refusal to attend the funeral of General de Gaulle. France and Canada have many reasons to maintain frank and sincere ties of friendship. Pettiness, spite, differences of opinion must not alter these ties. It can be said that this is a tempest in a teapot; 1 will answer that very often such tempests mark the beginning of useless hostilities.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister should speak frankly. He does not have any valid reasons to offer-as his silence implies-he should say so frankly. In the meantime, he can always draw inspiration by reading General de Gaulle's memoirs.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister and of his Parliamentary Secretary the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson), who are both presently attending a meeting here in Ottawa with representatives of the American government, I wanted to answer the hon. member for Champlain, but, after the Chair's two appropriate reminders, I think I have nothing to add.

maintopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PERFORMANCE OF ILLEGAL ABORTION ON PROGRAM "WEEKEND"
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-PERFORMANCE OF ILLEGAL ABORTION ON PROGRAM "WEEKEND"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) a three-part question regarding last evening's CBC "Weekend" program. For reasons known only to himself, the minister decided to ignore the question and not answer, but I hope an answer will be given this evening for I am sure that if the minister had seen this program he would have felt the same concern and disgust as I did. It is of little use to express this concern to the CBC's officials, Mr. Speaker, for these officials have even more disregard for the representations of citizens and MPs than the minister.
Part of the program in question to which I am objecting was the presentation of an abortion, beginning with a call from a girl in Vancouver to a Los Angeles abortion clinic, continuing with the surgical intervention, the vacuum suction procedure of the abortion, and ending with the post-surgical care to the patient. My first question, Mr. Speaker, is whether the performers in this presentation were paid directly or indirectly for their performance in a criminal, illegal abortion, but many more questions come to mind. Was the patient an ordi-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
nary individual really going through an abortion, or was she an actress? Were her abortion fees, air fare and other expenses paid with taxpayers' money? How was this young lady found, and how did the CBC stage the event? Did the doctors or the clinic receive any direct or indirect remuneration from the CBC? Was the program seen and/or approved by top CBC management?
At the end of the program the CBC announced a proposed opinion poll, the results to be shown next week. Mr. Speaker, I am curious to know if this poll will be taken to influence public opinion rather than report on it. Is the patient, coming from Vancouver, part of the diabolical plot involving that group of ignorant young ladies who gave Your Honour such a trying time and showed such disrespect for this House and the democratic process earlier this year?
Is this program part of such a plot to influence public opinion, or is it the reflection of sympathy by the producer and some CBC officials for the cause of free abortion? Their stupidity in contravening the proposed House of Commons debate by showing a program in such bad taste is morally offensive to very many Canadians. Mr. Speaker, the minister, I submit will be party to the connivance if he allows this report to be shown, probably after much editing, many staged interviews and the usual rating-affecting, distorted impact scenes have been taken. If the top CBC officials have any such control, then surely they are prostituting their mandate by agreeing to such programs.
The final part of my question, Mr. Speaker, asked the purpose for which this program was produced. Is the reason justifiable, or is this just another attempt by the CBC to influence program ratings by showing another program offensive to the morals of many Canadian viewers who pay for this nonsense? With each new, additional and questionable program of this type, Mr. Speaker, the goals, objectives and purposes of our national networks become more and more suspect. One network, the CBC, seems intent on the destruction of the moral values and fibre of our society. The other branch of the corporation, Radio Canada, seems intent on the destruction of our elected governmental bodies and our democratic system.
It is true that Parliament has given the top CBC management an autonomy which practically places this organization out of reach of all authority. Unless those responsible can stop delegating their authority to all sorts of irresponsible people down the line, and unless they have the courage and judgment to accept their responsibility and make the decisions necessary to stop this gross abuse of our national television system, they should resign. No program which offends the morals of people is justifiable, and this latest example goes much beyond the bounds of decency and objective programming.
I hope that the minister will insist on full answers and explanations with regard to these questions and will accept the duty inherent in his position of giving explanations to the House. I am supported, Mr. Speaker, in this submission by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Sullivan) and many other hon. members.

November 23, 1970
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Mr. James Hugh Faulkner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State): Mr. Speaker, the reply from the corporation is as follows: The question of legal abortion has been a matter of public interest for some time now. It was one of the questions discussed very recently at the Liberal party convention, and the CBC considers that the "Weekend" item was entirely justified. No performers were used in the item, nor were fees paid by the corporation to any of the participants. The CBC, however, did pay the American producers of the item in Los Angeles. The opinion poll commissioned by 'Weekend" will be carefully taken over a number of weeks, not just next week, to discover what public opinion is with regard to the question of abortion legislation.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.20 p.m.
